Analyze rhymes in song lyrics

Source: R/rhymes.R
analyze_rhymes.Rd

Detect assonance rhymes (matching vowel sounds) in lyrics and summarize how densely the lyrics rhyme. This is an R implementation of Raplyzer by Eric Malmi.

Usage

analyze_rhymes(
  x,
  lookback = 15,
  min_length = 2,
  remove_duplicates = TRUE,
  lyrics_col = "lyrics",
  pronunciation = c("auto", "espeak", "cmudict")
)

Source

Malmi, E. (2015). Raplyzer. https://github.com/ekQ/raplysaattori

Carnegie Mellon University. The CMU Pronouncing Dictionary. https://github.com/cmusphinx/cmudict

eSpeak NG. https://github.com/espeak-ng/espeak-ng

Arguments

x

Lyrics to analyze. Either a character vector, where each element is the full text of one song with lines separated by "\n", or a data frame with a list-column of lyrics, such as taylor_album_songs or taylor_all_songs. Each element of the list-column should be a data frame with a lyric column, with one row per line.

lookback

The number of previous words to search for a rhyme.

min_length

The minimum number of matching vowels to count as a rhyme.

remove_duplicates

Logical. Should duplicate lines (e.g., repeated choruses) be removed before analysis? Lines that are entirely within parentheses or brackets (e.g., backing vocals) are always removed.

lyrics_col

If x is a data frame, the name of the list-column that contains the lyrics.

pronunciation

Where pronunciations come from. One of "auto" (the default; eSpeak if it's installed, and otherwise the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary), "espeak", or "cmudict". See Details.

Value

A tibble. If x is a character vector, there is one row per element of x, with a text column containing the lyrics. If x is a data frame, x is returned with additional columns. In both cases, the following columns are included:

  • n_words: The number of words analyzed. Words without a vowel sound (e.g., "the" or "hmm") are not included.

  • total_rhymes: The number of words that rhyme with a previous word.

  • unique_rhymes: The number of distinct rhyming word pairs. For example, if "night" rhymes with "tonight" three times, that is one unique rhyme.

  • rhyme_density: The average rhyme length per word.

  • longest_rhyme_length: The number of vowels in the longest rhyme.

  • longest_rhyme: The two parts of the longest rhyme, separated by /.

Songs without any lyrics have missing values for all columns.

Details

Each word in the lyrics is converted to a sequence of vowel sounds. Consonants are ignored. For each word, the algorithm looks back at the previous lookback words and finds the longest matching sequence of vowels that ends with both words. The match starts at the last vowel of each word and continues backward, crossing word boundaries, until the first mismatch. For example, "bad blood" and "mad love" share two vowel sounds (the a in "bad" and "mad", and the u in "blood" and "love"), so they form a rhyme of length 2. A word can't rhyme with an identical word, and a match stops when it reaches a pair of identical words (e.g., "cold as you" and "so as to" form a rhyme of length 1, because the match stops at the repeated "as"). Rhymes shorter than min_length vowels are ignored.

The rhyme density is the average rhyme length across all words, not counting the first word. Higher values mean more (and longer) rhymes. Raplyzer reported a rhyme density of 0.95 for Shakespeare's poems and 0.92 for the musical Hamilton. However, those values aren't directly comparable to the values from this function, because of the differences described below.

Pronunciation

Like the original Raplyzer, pronunciations can come from the eSpeak speech synthesizer, which must be installed separately. If eSpeak isn't installed, pronunciations come from the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary, which is included in the package. Words not in the dictionary get a rough pronunciation from their spelling. By default (pronunciation = "auto"), eSpeak is used if it's installed. The two sources mostly agree, but results can differ slightly, so set pronunciation explicitly if you need results that are reproducible across computers. eSpeak is found by looking for espeak-ng and then espeak on the PATH, or you can set the path with options(taylor.espeak = "path/to/espeak").

With either source, numbers are first converted to words the way they are typically spoken (e.g., "22" becomes "twenty two", "1989" becomes "nineteen eighty nine", and "2AM" becomes "two eh em").

Differences from Raplyzer

This implementation differs from the original Raplyzer in a few ways:

  • Each word is transcribed by itself, rather than in the context of the full lyrics, and similar vowels are grouped the same way for both pronunciation sources.

  • Diphthongs (e.g., the vowel in "night") are treated as a single vowel, so "night" doesn't rhyme with "trap kit".

  • Words are considered identical when they're spelled the same, rather than when they're pronounced the same.

Examples

bad_blood <- paste(
  "Cause, baby, now we got bad blood",
  "You know it used to be mad love",
  sep = "\n"
)
analyze_rhymes(bad_blood)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   text     n_words total_rhymes unique_rhymes rhyme_density longest_rhyme_length
#>   <chr>      <int>        <int>         <int>         <dbl>                <int>
#> 1 "Cause,…      15            1             1         0.143                    2
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: longest_rhyme <chr>

fearless <- taylor_album_songs[taylor_album_songs$album_name == "Fearless", ]
analyze_rhymes(fearless)
